questions.q: What is the primary defining feature of a parliamentary system of government regarding the relationship between the executive and the legislature?
questions.a: In a parliamentary system, the executive is drawn from and remains accountable to the legislature. A student who answers that the executive and legislature operate completely independently reveals a misunderstanding, confusing the parliamentary model with the presidential system (like the USA) where powers are strictly separated.

questions.q: Why does the Indian Constitution establish a parliamentary system instead of separating the executive and legislature entirely into two isolated branches?
questions.a: The parliamentary system is chosen to ensure continuous democratic accountability, where the government must face elected representatives every day and can be removed through a majority vote of no-confidence. A student who thinks it is chosen just to save money or time shows a lack of understanding of political accountability and democratic checks and balances.

questions.q: During a session of Parliament, an opposition MP asks the Minister of Railways about train safety protocols, and the minister must stand up and answer. Which key feature of the parliamentary system does this scenario demonstrate?
questions.a: This demonstrates executive accountability to the legislature, where ministers are responsible for their departments and must answer questions from elected representatives. A student who claims this shows judicial supremacy misinterprets which organ of government is exercising oversight over the executive branch.

questions.q: How does the composition of the Council of Ministers in a parliamentary system differ from the membership of the legislature?
questions.a: While all members of the Council of Ministers (the executive) must be or become members of Parliament (the legislature), not all members of Parliament are ministers; most MPs serve as lawmakers, scrutinizers, and representatives without holding executive office portfolios. A student who believes the executive and legislature consist of entirely different sets of people fails to grasp the overlap characteristic of parliamentary systems.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument that a parliamentary system is more unstable than a presidential system because the government can fall if it loses a single majority vote in the legislature.
questions.a: While a parliamentary system can experience political instability or coalition breakdowns leading to early elections, this structural feature prioritizes supreme democratic responsiveness over fixed terms, allowing the nation to rapidly change leadership if public mandate shifts. A student who argues it is completely flawed overlooks how this mechanism prevents autocratic rule by forcing the executive to maintain continuous legislative support.

questions.q: Design a short parliamentary rule or question format that could be used by MPs to hold the executive accountable for environmental pollution in major cities.
questions.a: A strong student design would propose a mandatory weekly "Environmental Accountability Hour" where the Environment Minister must present pollution reduction data and face direct questioning from MPs representing affected constituencies. A weak answer would merely suggest punishing polluting factories without mentioning parliamentary oversight, missing the core concept of institutional accountability.
